title: Discrete Measure of Asymmetry Through Minimal Symmetric Completion and Its Applications in Physics, Engineering and Biology
content: We introduce a new geometric parameter to characterize symmetry of a set of 2D points: the measure of asymmetry equal to the minimum number of points that must be added to make a pattern symmetric, while keeping all original points unchanged. A pattern that already possesses the required symmetry has zero asymmetry. Unlike continuous symmetry measures, which describe how far points must move to achieve symmetry, the proposed parameter counts missing symmetry partners. We develop this approach for mirror and rotational symmetries and establish exact methods for finding the smallest completion. Any planar set containing at least two distinct points can acquire mirror symmetry by adding no more than the original number of points minus two. For randomly distributed points, we determine how the minimum number of additions depends on the order of rotational symmetry. We also apply the approach to crystals containing vacancies. The number of vacancies does not always equal the asymmetry measure, because some arrangements of vacancies preserve symmetry. We identify the conditions under which the two quantities coincide and relate the mean asymmetry to temperature through equilibrium vacancy statistics. This framework offers a direct way to quantify missing elements needed to restore symmetry, with potential applications to materials, engineering arrays, and biological patterns.
